commits.summary: Regression proofs share the callees both versions call unchanged, and skip a target whose bytecode is identical (verification pending)
commits.body:
jvmcontract equivalence now compares the two versions' bytecode before any solver runs (lib/src/shared.rs). A target identical in both versions, together with everything it reaches (instructions compared with their constant pool references resolved, exception tables, the static initializers and constant values of the classes whose statics it reads), is verified with nothing to prove and no JBMC run. A callee both versions call unchanged, that is a pure function of its primitive arguments (no fields, no arrays, nothing of the JDK beyond Math/StrictMath/Integer/Long/Short/Byte, string building and the exceptions it constructs), is taken as one function in both versions, the uninterpreted-function abstraction of regression verification: a generated stub class (SharedCallees, the class writer now writes static fields) keeps a memo table per callee, giving arguments seen before the outcome they got and new arguments an arbitrary result or one of the exceptions the callee can throw (its new'ed Throwables, plus ArithmeticException where it divides), and the invokestatic call sites of both versions are redirected to it by appending constant pool entries and rewriting the operands in place. The solver then relates how the versions use the callee and never its arithmetic. The abstraction is sound for a proof; a counterexample found with it is replayed through the real bytecode and, when it does not reproduce, the proof is run again with the callees as written, with a note. --no-shared-callees turns both off. The proof line names the callees taken as one function; Outcome gains a shared field.

Why: a 64-bit division in a helper both versions call was what turned a regression proof of a caller into a time-out, since each version carried its own copy for the solver to relate. Measured: a refactor of a caller around a division helper went from not finishing in 60 s to a proof in 0.2 s, and HoldPolicy-style pricing with Math.multiplyExact shared from 3.4 s to 0.4 s.

Example 120 on Crosscut: a new kernel, ratelimit.RetryAfter#nanosUntilToken (the Retry-After of a refused request, from TokenBucket's refill helpers), with a test, a property proved in 1.7 s, and the API contract regenerated; the example's patch rewrites the wait as the period less the time since the credit, around the unchanged helpers. By hand: proved in 1.3 s with the helpers shared; without sharing the [-100000:100000] search stage had not finished after 60 s. New technique tag shared-callees. Job 20261104-054836-example-120-a-retry-after-rewrite-proved queued (build.py on the example). Docs: lib README (proof steps and limits), approaches.md B9, the Crosscut README, the plugin reference; build.py reads the 'nothing to prove' proof line.

commits.summary: Regression proofs across a signature change: the previous version named and called with expressions over the new parameters (verification pending)
commits.body:
jvmcontract equivalence proved a method only against a previous version of the same name and parameters; a method renamed, moved, or whose parameters were reordered, added, removed or retyped could not be proved at all. Now --before-target names the previous method (pkg.Class#method) and --before-arguments gives its arguments as expressions over the new parameters (tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB; start, (int) (end - start), failed; an array by name), and the statement proved is new(x) agrees with old(f(x)). The harness (lib/src/harness/mod.rs, BeforeMethod) type-checks each expression against the parameter it is passed as with the expression language's call syntax, narrows for byte/short/char and widens for long, computes the arguments into locals inside a handler that skips an input the mapping throws on, and calls the relocated previous method; the Java rendering shows the mapping. equivalence.rs resolves the previous method in the old classes and refuses clearly when the class or method is missing, is not static, returns another type, or when the parameters differ with no mapping given; the proof line reads 'behaves as the previous winner(tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB) on every input', a counterexample is shown as both versions received it ('winner(tsA=0, tsB=0, nodeA=0, nodeB=0), previously winner(tsA=0, nodeA=0, tsB=0, nodeB=0)'), the replay maps the arguments through the interpreter, and the JSON outcome carries the previous call. shared::plan takes both targets and uses the identical-bytecode shortcut only for the plain statement, since f(a, b) against f(b, a) on identical bytecode proves nothing. The tool's own checker handles the mapped harness unchanged.

Example 121 (B9, Quorum): LastWriterWins#winner regrouped as (tsA, tsB, nodeA, nodeB) and written as a Long.compare/Integer.compare chain, with the test and the law in properties.contract updated in the patch; example.json carries change.previousArguments, which build.py passes to the tool (change.previousSymbol maps to --before-target; schema and page rendering extended); new technique tag signature-change. Job 20261104-061118-example-121-a-tie-break-s-parameters-reg is queued. Verified: 97 unit tests (one new, the harness with a mapping) and 37 integration tests (four new on a Writers fixture: a reordering proved, a moved and renamed method proved, a tie rewrite found with the mapped counterexample, a refusal without a mapping), clippy clean on the changed files, the patched Quorum tree compiles and its 58 tests pass, the mapped proof and counterexample reproduced under --engine native, release binary installed. Documented in lib/README.md, the plugin reference, examples/approaches.md, examples/README.md and Quorum's README.

commits.summary: Regression proofs under a stated relation between the results: a result that changed its type or meaning is related to the previous one with --results-agree-when (verification pending)
commits.body:
A regression proof compared what the two versions return, so a method whose return type changed, or whose result changed its meaning (a boolean that became the time left, nanoseconds that became milliseconds), could not be proved against its previous version. jvmcontract equivalence now takes --results-agree-when EXPR, a boolean expression over the new parameters, previous (the previous version's result) and result (the new one's), which takes the place of equality whenever both versions return; the versions must still throw alike, array parameters are still compared, and a relation that throws on a pair of results does not hold. The expression is type-checked against both return types, compiled into the generated harness (lib/src/harness/mod.rs, BeforeMethod::parse_relation, Harness.relation) and rendered in the Java statement written for readers. Differing return types are refused without a relation, with a message that names the flag. The identical-bytecode shortcut and the shared-callee plan are off under a relation, since identical code proves nothing about it. A counterexample is replayed in the interpreter and the relation evaluated on the replayed results (lib/src/equivalence.rs, Replays), so that a JBMC counterexample a missing model produced is still recognised as not reproducing; the report adds the line 'the results are not related by ...' under the two outcomes, and the JSON outcome carries the relation.

Examples 122 and 123 on Crosscut's cache expiry: Expiry#isExpired, a boolean, turned into the time an entry has left, related by previousSymbol and resultsAgreeWhen 'previous == (result <= 0)' with the module's own precondition as the scope (outside it the new subtraction overflows). 123 (remainingNanos) is expected verified; 122 (remainingMillis) is expected to show an entry with a fraction of a millisecond to go reported expired, since the integer division rounds it to no millisecond. The example runner passes change.resultsAgreeWhen to the tool (examples/tools/build.py, examples/schema/example.schema.json), and the pages, lib/README.md, examples/approaches.md, the Crosscut README and the verify-bytecode skill reference describe the flag. Jobs 20261104-063213-example-122-a-cache-expiry-in-millisecon and 20261104-063213-example-123-a-cache-expiry-turned-from-a.

commits.summary: The tool's own checker looks for a violating input in JBMC's stages, so its witnesses read as JBMC's; examples 124 and 125 run regression proofs through it (verification pending)
commits.body:
The native bounded model checker (lib/src/bmc) returned the first model the SAT solver gave for a violating path, which for three 64-bit values the interpreter's shrinker did not bring down (example 122's second note). It now asks, on each violating path, for an input in the ranges JBMC is run through, [0:20], then [-100000:100000], then everything, and reports the stage in the proof line as JBMC does (searching inputs in [0:20]). A path that fails only on large values does not end the search: the remaining paths are explored for as long again as the first violation took, within the deadline, in case one of them fails in a smaller stage, and any stop after a violation is found (budget, a loop beyond the bound, something outside the fragment) returns the violation. A proof pays nothing: the range literals are built at the first violation. Unit tests cover the stage chosen per shape (an overflow in the second stage, a single large value in none, a small-value path found after a large-value one, a long and a boolean), and that the stages spell JBMC's; the millisecond Expiry integration test now also runs the tool's own checker and expects the same shrunk witness and the stage in its output.

Examples 124 and 125 (Crosscut, B9) are run by the tool's own checker: approach.engine (schema enum jbmc/native/auto) becomes build.py's --engine on B9 and B11 of the javac apps, the proof-line regexes accept the checker's line, and the findings text names the checker that proved it. 124 rewrites kafka.Partitioner#partitionFor with Math.floorMod: the property of example 023 still holds and the tests pass, but every negative hash moves partition; the library's run found the difference in the second stage in 0.4 s and shrank it to partitionFor(hash=-1, numPartitions=3), 1 before and 2 after. 125 moves JwtTimestamps#valid's skew from the window's ends to the clock under the module's precondition as the scope, proved in 0.3 s over eleven paths; without the scope the versions differ on an overflow, with a witness no stage contains. New tags: routing-change (defect) and own-checker (technique). Both patches apply, both patched trees compile and pass the 42 Crosscut tests. Jobs 20261104-064900-example-124-a-partitioner-rewritten-with and 20261104-064900-example-125-a-jwt-skew-moved-from-the-wi are queued.

commits.summary: Regression proofs on a record's components: a method of a record, or one taking or returning a record of primitives, is proved with the record built from symbolic components in both versions; examples 126 and 127 on a new backoff kernel (verification pending)
commits.body:
Until now a regression proof took static methods over primitives and arrays, and an instance method or a record parameter was refused. The harness now lays the target out over flat parameters (harness::Layout): a record whose components are all primitive, as the receiver, a parameter or the result, becomes its components, named this.component or parameter.component, which JBMC chooses symbolically. The harness builds the record from them in each version through its canonical constructor, inside handlers for every exception class it tells apart (JBMC matches a handler by the exception's own class, so a catch of Throwable alone does not take a stub IllegalArgumentException), so that an input a constructor of either version rejects is outside the statement and the proof is over the record's invariant; it calls an instance method with invokevirtual on each version's receiver, and compares a record result component by component from the fields of each version's record. The previous version's descriptor is relocated under before/ for the call and the replay, the witness is written as Java prints a record (delayMillis(this=Backoff[baseMillis=1, capMillis=1], attempt=-1)), the interpreter replay constructs the records and dispatches on the receiver, and the domain reads this: Backoff(baseMillis: long, capMillis: long) × attempt: int. A scope or relation may name a component as the method does (baseMillis) or as this.baseMillis. A target identical in both versions is verified without a proof only when the records' constructors are identical too. Refused with a reason: a record with a non-primitive component, components that changed between the versions, a static method that became a record's method or the reverse, and a record parameter passed to the previous version by an expression. The tool's own checker has no objects and hands such a harness to JBMC under auto. build.py passes approach.unwind as --unwind, for a loop that needs more than the default sixteen turns.

Examples 126 and 127 are on a new Crosscut kernel, retry.Backoff, a record of a base and a cap whose delayMillis(attempt) doubles the base up to the cap by a loop, with a compact constructor that keeps the base positive and the cap between the base and a day. 126 replaces the loop by Math.min(capMillis, baseMillis << attempt), which the tests pass and the proof refutes: the inline run found delayMillis(this=Backoff[baseMillis=1, capMillis=1], attempt=-1), the loop returning 1 and the shift Long.MIN_VALUE, in 1.9 s, and scoped to attempts 0 to 62 the overflow at a base of 32 and 58 attempts. 127 replaces the loop by the shift kept below the base's leading zeros, which the inline run proved equal in 6.2 s with the loop unwound 32 times. Jobs 20261104-071749-example-126-a-backoff-s-doubling-loop-re and 20261104-071749-example-127-a-backoff-s-doubling-loop-re are queued. Verified with 102 unit tests (two new: the layout and harness over a record receiver, argument and result; dotted component names in expressions) and 44 integration tests (four new, through JBMC: a record's method proved on its components, the overflowing shift refuted and proved under a scope naming a component, a record result compared component by component, and a changed constructor keeping an identical method from the no-proof shortcut), clippy with nothing new, the release binary installed, both patches applied and the three Crosscut trees compiled and passing their 45 tests. Docs: lib/README.md (the proof's steps, what is new, limits), examples/approaches.md, examples/README.md, the verify-bytecode reference, the Crosscut README, tags.json (technique record-components), the example schema (approach.unwind).

commits.summary: Regression proofs relate a record result whose components changed, or a result that became a record, by a relation over the components; examples 134 and 135 on a new window-counter kernel of Crosscut (verification pending)
commits.body:
A record result of other components than before, or a result that is a record in one version and a primitive in the other, had no way into a regression proof: there was no expression for the previous result. Now --results-agree-when takes the components of a record result by name, previous.c and result.c (harness::Layout.result is the pair of the two versions' result records, BeforeMethod::parse_relation names each record's components in slots of their own, and the generated harness reads them from the two results by getfield before the relation; two null records agree, one null alone does not; the statement as Java prints them as accessor calls). Without a relation the tool refuses and proposes one over the components the records share by name and type. A replayed counterexample reads the components back from the interpreter's object (witness::Replayed.result_fields) to check the relation and to show both records.

Examples 134 and 135 are regression proofs on a new kernel of Crosscut, ratelimit.Window, a fixed-window request counter whose counter is a record the method returns, across the record gaining a previousCount component for the sliding-window estimate: 134 advances the start by exactly one window instead of aligning it to the clock, found by JBMC in a fraction of a second within aligned starts as the scope (the witness a request two windows ahead of an empty counter); 135 keeps the alignment and is proved equal on the start and the count on every input by the tool's own checker in 12 s, where JBMC did not finish within a minute. Jobs 20261104-085102-example-134-a-window-counter-that-advanc and 20261104-085102-example-135-a-window-counter-with-the-pr are queued.

Verified by a new unit test on the harness (the components' slots, the getfield reads, the Java statement), a new integration test cross-checking the verified, violated, became-a-record and refused cases with JBMC (4 s), the full suite (106 unit, 50 integration tests), the Crosscut app's 49 tests on the base tree and on both patched trees, both patches applying, and the four proof runs inline with both engines.

commits.summary: The tool's own checker leaves a multiplication to the solver under cheap facts and rewrites a quotient times its divisor as the dividend less the remainder; examples 138 and 139 on the window start as the window's index times its length (verification pending)
commits.body:
The own bounded model checker (lib/src/bmc) extends last cycle's lazy division to multiplication: a product of two non-constant values is fresh bits under what holds of every product modulo the width (a factor of zero gives zero, of one the other factor, of minus one its negation, a power of two shifts by its exponent, the low eight bits are exact), a model that gets a product wrong has the multiplier built and tied to the bits, and products of the same operands in either order are the same bits. A quotient times its divisor is rewritten exactly as the dividend less the remainder, (a / b) * b as a - a % b, which holds in two's complement for every pair including a division by zero and MIN_VALUE / -1, so the identity between a 64-bit division and multiplication that neither engine proved within a minute is the same bits on both sides. The log line now counts divisions and multiplications separately.

Example 131's loop of delay *= multiplier, proved in 22 s with its 27 multipliers built, takes 4 s with none built (release build, 1.19M clauses down to 385k); 130 goes from 1.5 s to 1.1 s; the other own-checker examples (120, 124, 125, 128, 129, 132, 134 to 137) are unchanged. The divide-and-multiply form of the window alignment, out of reach of both engines last cycle, is proved in 0.1 s, and the credited-time rewrite that example 133's last note recorded as out of reach in 0.3 s; the notes of 120, 131, 133 and 137 say so.

Example 138 is the window counter's start computed as the window's index times its length, long index = nowNanos / windowNanos; long start = index * windowNanos, proved equal to the remainder form on every input by the own checker in 0.1 s where JBMC does not finish within 60 s. Example 139 holds the index in an int: at a reading of 2^31 windows the cast wraps, the start is negative, and the record's constructor refuses it, so every request from then on throws; found in 3 s as counted(this=Window[startNanos=0, count=0], nowNanos=2147483648, windowNanos=1), JBMC >60 s. Pipeline jobs 20261104-094056-example-138-window-start-as-the-window-s and 20261104-094056-example-139-window-index-held-in-an-int.

Verified with three new unit tests (the facts prove a product by zero, one and a power of two with no circuit, a wrong product of the same low bits is refined once, the quotient-times-divisor rewrite gives the same bits and holds at MIN_VALUE / -1, an engine run that is verified with 0 of 1 products built and one refuted with the real product), 112 unit and 50 integration tests passing, the Crosscut app's 48 tests on both patched trees, both patches applying, and the release binary installed.

commits.summary: build.py: how a verifier's run ended is decided before its verdict (verification pending)
commits.body:
Step 1a of the build-orchestration brief. Before, build.py classified a jvmcontract or Java-verifier run as verified on exit 0, unverifiable when the output said 'cannot be verified', and violation otherwise. A verifier killed by signal 9 with empty output was recorded as 'Violation: counterexample found', with no counterexample, and matched an example that expected a violation. write_evidence() also wrote an empty SARIF report when the verifier wrote none. The review's findings were checked against the code at c4fa2f64 and all still held.

Now execution_status() and conclude() (and tlc_conclusion() for TLC, run directly for Box Office or through jvmcontract tlc --json) first record result.execution: completed, timed-out, killed (a negative code or 128+N), invalid-output (nothing printed, malformed JSON, exit 1 with no evidence or no report) or tool-error (any other exit code; a TLC run that ended without a verdict). Only a completed run has a verdict. A violation needs the evidence the runner read (counterexamples, changed cases, capability or boundary changes, new ! lines, a trace) and the verifier's SARIF report. A run without a verdict records verdict null, the label '⚠ No verdict: <reason>' and expectation not-evaluable, and matchesExpected is false. build.py exits 1 and prints a line the pipeline's example:unexpected signal matches. The runs that give the verdict are recorded, not fatal, on exit code 2. Setup steps (update, tla, compile) still stop the runner, now also on a signal. A missing report is not made up, and a stale result.sarif or statement.java from an earlier run is removed, so a folder never shows another run's evidence. Each D1 configuration also records its status. The page of a run without a verdict says so in place of the findings.

Choices: a run that did not complete gets verdict null, not 'unverifiable'. That is the option that reports less, and otherwise a crash would match example 003, which expects unverifiable.
